text: Social engineering is the psychological manipulation of a person into taking an action or revealing information that compromises security. None of these techniques exploit a software flaw — a firewall and strong encryption do nothing to stop an attack aimed at someone's trust or curiosity, which is exactly why social engineering remains one of the most effective ways into an organization.

Phishing is a fraudulent email sent to a large number of recipients, impersonating a trusted sender to trick someone into clicking a link or entering credentials. It's a numbers game — the attacker doesn't need everyone to fall for it. Spear phishing narrows that down to one researched target. Pretexting builds a fabricated scenario or false identity to manipulate someone into divulging information. And baiting dangles something enticing, like a labeled USB drive, that delivers a compromise the moment someone takes it.

The difference between phishing and spear phishing comes down to volume versus precision. A generic phishing blast only needs a tiny fraction of thousands of recipients to click. Spear phishing invests real research into one target — their name, their job, their vendors — which takes more effort but succeeds far more often. That's the technique behind most high-value business email compromise incidents.

Picture a pretexting call to the help desk: the caller claims to be a traveling VP who's locked out, frames it as urgent, leans on the authority of that title, and asks for a password reset with no verification. Each piece does its own work — the pretext gives a plausible reason, the urgency discourages double-checking, and the authority pressures the help desk to comply anyway.

Technical controls get patched. Human trust, curiosity, and urgency don't patch the same way, because they're part of normal behavior attackers deliberately exploit. That's why awareness training and callback verification on urgent requests matter as much as any firewall rule. Next up: network attacks — man-in-the-middle, denial of service, and spoofing — where the target shifts from the person to the network itself.
